title: Orellana's descent of the Amazon
summary: On 26 December 1541 Francisco de Orellana, second-in-command of Gonzalo Pizarro's expedition, set off down the Napo River with about 50 men to find food. They followed the Napo into the Amazon, reached the Negro River on 3 June 1542 and the open sea in late August, and arrived at the Spanish island of Cubagua in early September 1542. The chaplain Gaspar de Carvajal recorded the voyage.

uncertainty.note: Open sea reached 24 or 26 August 1542; Cubagua 9 September (San Pedro) or 11 September (Victoria) per Brewminate; Encyclopedia.com says early September.

reviewer_note: December 1541 and June 1542 dates rest on Brewminate alone (class other). Brewminate gives 24 or 26 August 1542 for the open sea; the Atlantic mouth is not a waypoint (no coordinate source). Encyclopedia.com says about 60 men or 50 soldiers; Brewminate says about 50 then 49. Napo and Negro positions are loose (300 km uncertainty). Wikidata gives two coordinates for the Napo with unlabelled qualifiers; the first is used. Open Rivers (UMN) says the journey ran from the Andes to Marajo Island at the Atlantic, begins on the Napo, and that Carvajal described large populations and roads; Brewminate lists Omagua, Machiparo people, Pira-tapuya and Tapuya groups. Name Amazon: Encyclopedia.com says the Spaniards first named the land after Greek Amazons, the river later; Brewminate notes the link is uncertain.

beats.caption: On 26 December 1541 Orellana leaves Pizarro's party on the Napo with about 50 men, searching downstream for food.
The boats reach the Negro River on 3 June 1542; Carvajal later describes large Indigenous settlements along the banks.
Reaching Cubagua in September 1542, the chaplain's tale of tall women fighters leads the Spaniards to link the land to the Greek Amazons.
